name: Frutiger Aero

lead: Frutiger Aero is an internet aesthetic that grew out of 2000s interface design. It features glossy, translucent surfaces, bright blues and greens, water, sky, grass and bubbles, and a hopeful picture of technology living in harmony with nature.

For appearance, it is a style reference. People use it to guide fresh, clean, glossy looks in photos, makeup, nails, clothing and room or profile aesthetics. It is documented through design writing and journalism, and a 2026 preprint maps it among other internet aesthetics.

paras: People recreate the look with bright aqua and green palettes, glossy or dewy finishes, translucent accessories and nature-and-tech imagery in photos, edits and outfits. It is also used to style social media profiles and digital collages. No special products are required; it is a mood board rather than a routine.
There are no health risks from the aesthetic itself. Products used to get glossy finishes carry their own usual considerations.

lead: Frutiger Aero is a design style and internet aesthetic that was prevalent from the mid-2000s to the early 2010s. It pairs technology with natural imagery, using bright colors, glossy reflective textures and skeuomorphic elements.[1] The name was coined in 2018 by Sofi Xian of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute, combining the Frutiger typeface with the Windows Aero interface language.[1]

Interest in it revived in 2023 and 2024, especially among Gen Z users who experience it as nostalgic, and it spread on YouTube and TikTok.[1] Its visual vocabulary of blue skies, water, grass, bubbles and gloss is used as inspiration for fresh, luminous styling in photos, makeup and fashion. Academic work has begun to map it among other internet aesthetics: a 2026 preprint reconstructs a network of 1,115 aesthetics from community cross-referencing and names Frutiger Aero among them.[2]

paras: The style is marked by vibrant blues, greens and yellows, three-dimensional graphics, glossy and reflective textures, and skeuomorphism, especially in app icons. Common motifs include blue skies, grass, auroras, lens flares and bokeh, along with water and tropical fish. In interiors it appears as translucent glass and acrylic.[1]

It followed the Y2K aesthetic, and most scholars date its peak to roughly 2004-2013. Windows Vista (2006) was among the first examples and Windows 7 (2009) expanded it, with the first iPhone (2007) and Samsung Galaxy S (2010) cited as device examples. It declined in the early 2010s as flat design replaced it.[1]
During its peak it had no common name; the retrospective label "Web 2.0 Gloss" was also used.[1]

Writers linked the 2023-2024 revival to nostalgia and, in one account, to the AI boom; others describe it as an alternative to minimalist interfaces, and Apple's 2025 Liquid Glass design was described as likely influenced by it.[1] Le Monde described it as nostalgia for a "Garden of Eden", and researchers group it with a fascination with outdated futures.[1]
Online, creators apply the look in outfit, makeup and photo-edit styles built around aqua tones, gloss and nature imagery. These uses are community practice rather than a documented procedure.
No studies found. A 2026 preprint on the network of internet aesthetics, which lists Frutiger Aero, studied how aesthetics relate to one another rather than any effect on appearance.[2]
